title: Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction and Polarization
subcategory: Wave Optics — Young's Double Slit, Diffraction, Polarization

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 12 — Wave Optics

summary: Interference (from two coherent sources) and diffraction (bending of light around obstacles/through narrow openings) are both consequences of light's wave nature (superposition), while polarization — restricting a transverse wave's vibration to one plane — is possible only because light is a transverse wave, distinguishing it from longitudinal waves like sound.
explanation: Young's double-slit experiment demonstrated that light shows interference: two coherent sources (constant phase relationship, same frequency — obtained in practice from a single source split into two, since two independent sources are never perfectly coherent) produce alternating bright (constructive interference, path difference = nλ) and dark (destructive interference, path difference = (n+½)λ) fringes on a screen, with fringe width β = λD/d (D = slit-to-screen distance, d = slit separation). Diffraction is the bending of waves around obstacles or spreading through narrow apertures, becoming significant when the aperture/obstacle size is comparable to the wavelength — this is why sound (long wavelength) diffracts noticeably around corners in everyday life, while light's diffraction (much shorter wavelength) is only obvious with very narrow slits. A single-slit diffraction pattern has a wide, bright central maximum flanked by much dimmer secondary maxima, distinctly different from the EQUALLY spaced, EQUALLY bright fringes of double-slit interference. Polarization restricts the vibration of a transverse wave's electric field to a single plane; since polarization is only possible for TRANSVERSE waves (not longitudinal), the fact that light can be polarized was itself historical evidence that light is a transverse wave. Malus's law gives the intensity after passing through a polaroid: I = I₀cos²θ, where θ is the angle between the polarizer's transmission axis and the incoming polarization direction. The key structural difference between interference and diffraction: interference results from a small (usually two) number of coherent sources with EQUAL intensity, EQUALLY spaced, EQUALLY bright fringes, while diffraction results from secondary wavelets from a continuous single slit/obstacle, with UNEQUAL width and UNEQUAL (rapidly decreasing) intensity of fringes.
commonMisconceptions: Treating interference and diffraction as entirely separate/unrelated phenomena — both fundamentally arise from the superposition principle applied to waves; the distinction is more about the SOURCE configuration (few discrete coherent sources vs. a continuous distribution of wavelets from one aperture) than the underlying physics.

Assuming any two independent light bulbs can show a stable interference pattern — genuine sustained interference needs COHERENT sources (constant phase difference), which independent everyday sources never provide, since they emit light with a randomly varying phase.
Believing sound waves can be polarized just like light — polarization is possible only for TRANSVERSE waves; sound is longitudinal and cannot be polarized.
examples: Young's double-slit experiment with monochromatic light produces evenly spaced bright and dark fringes on a screen — direct evidence of light's wave nature.
Polaroid sunglasses block strongly polarized glare (e.g., reflected off water or roads) because their transmission axis is oriented to reject that particular polarization direction.
genZNote: Interference and diffraction: both wave superposition flexing, just with a different guest list of sources.
